newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Cocoa pressers reject Dutch study on fats proposal.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa pressers reject Dutch study on fats proposal.

text.p: Europe's cocoa pressers rejected on Wednesday the findings of a recent scientific study at Amsterdam University which found the likely impact of the EU vegetable fat proposal less than initially thought.
The Brussels-based Cocoa Campaign, an association of cocoa pressers in Europe, said it disagreed with the conclusions.
"We reject the findings of the report," spokesman for the Cocoa Campaign Thierry Lebeaux told Reuters.
The report, written by Kees Burger of the Economic and Social Institute, was partly funded by CAOBISCO, the Association of Chocololate, Biscuit and Confectionery Industries in the EU.

The report concluded that the effects of the European Union proposal to allow members to use up to five percent vegetable fat in chocolate production would have a smaller impact on the cocoa price and revenues of cocoa producers than first thought.
One of the report's initial assumptions contested by the Cocoa Campaign was that cocoa butter equivalents were in general around 15 percent cheaper than butter.
Lebeaux said there were far cheaper alternatives available.
"If you use palm oil for example, this is about one tenth of the price of cocoa butter," he said.

He added in an analysis of the UK market, the report ignored that many companies only produce chocolate using only cocoa butter because of their reliance on export markets. If the proposal was adopted, many more firms than envisaged in the report would switch to using substitutes, he said.
Lebeaux said the campaign also disagreed with the assumption that France and Italy were unlikely to adopt the directive.
"This is a misunderstanding. Palm oil is so much cheaper and the competitve edge of those who will use it will be so great that in the end everybody will switch," he said.
